entities.name: Justinian I
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Justinian I (c. 482–565 CE) was Byzantine Emperor from 527 to 565 whose ambitious reign reshaped law, architecture, and the boundaries of the Roman world. His codification of Roman law—the Corpus Juris Civilis (534 CE)—became the foundation of legal systems across Europe and remains the basis of civil law in dozens of countries today.

Born a Latin-speaking peasant in Illyria, Justinian rose through his uncle Justin I's patronage. With his formidable wife Theodora—a former actress—he pursued three grand projects: reconquering the lost Western Roman territories, systematizing Roman law, and building architectural monuments.

His general Belisarius reconquered North Africa from the Vandals (533–534), Italy from the Ostrogoths (535–554), and southern Spain from the Visigoths, briefly reuniting much of the old Roman Empire. Justinian commissioned the Hagia Sophia (537), whose revolutionary dome remained the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years.

The Plague of Justinian (541–542)—the first recorded bubonic plague pandemic—killed an estimated 25–50 million people and devastated his empire's economy and military. Despite this catastrophe, Justinian's legal and architectural legacy endured far beyond Byzantium. As the historian Procopius recorded: 'He transformed the whole state of the Romans.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Justinian's codification of Roman law and reconquest of Western territories reshaped the boundaries of the Roman world, influencing the development of civil law in dozens of countries. His legacy can be seen in the enduring institutions and legal systems of Europe.
